explanations.explanation: The mustache, friend. Verse 24 says Mephibosheth, Saul's grandson, had not cared for his feet or trimmed his mustache or washed his clothes from the day the king left until the day he returned safely. I know a thing or two about a mustache nobody manages, because mine has a mind of its own and it's also my hands. So he shows up to meet the king looking like he skipped every one of those.

The verse doesn't say a word about whether he talked to anyone. What it lists is his feet, his mustache and his clothes. And he's about to do plenty of talking, because the king asks him a question right away.

The text says nothing about where he slept. The verse sticks to three things: his feet, his mustache and his clothes. I think you were picturing a rough stretch, and the verse does say he hadn't looked after himself in that time.

explanations.answer: Why did you not go with me
explanations.explanation: That's the question, friend. David asks, “Mephibosheth, why did you not go with me?” It's short and it goes straight at the point. Mephibosheth has a lot to say in reply.

David doesn't ask where Ziba is. He asks Mephibosheth why he didn't go with him. Ziba does come up, though, in Mephibosheth's answer. He's Mephibosheth's servant, and Mephibosheth has plenty to say about him.

explanations.answer: Who told you I was coming
explanations.explanation: David never asks who told Mephibosheth anything. His question is “Mephibosheth, why did you not go with me?” It's like a text that just says, 'Where were you?' No small talk, no warm-up.

Donkey is right. Mephibosheth says, “I will have my donkey saddled so that I may ride on it and go with the king.” He gives it right after saying he is lame. So in his telling, he had a plan to get there.

A horse sounds fancy, but the verse says donkey. Mephibosheth says, “I will have my donkey saddled so that I may ride on it and go with the king.” That's the animal he names. Sometimes the humble answer is the one in the text.
A camel is a lot of animal to saddle up, friend. But Mephibosheth says donkey. He says, “I will have my donkey saddled so that I may ride on it and go with the king.” That's the one he names.

Mephibosheth says the opposite. He tells the king, “But my servant Ziba deceived me, and he has slandered your servant to my lord the king.” So in his words, Ziba lied and spoke against him. That's the story he brings to David.

False, and Mephibosheth says it plainly. He tells David, “But my servant Ziba deceived me, and he has slandered your servant to my lord the king.” He says Ziba deceived him and slandered him. That's the story he puts in front of the king.

explanations.answer: Do what is good in his eyes
explanations.explanation: That's his request. Mephibosheth says, “Yet my lord the king is like the angel of God, so do what is good in your eyes.” He doesn't hand David a list of demands. He puts the decision in the king's hands.

He says Ziba deceived and slandered him, but he never asks the king to punish him. What he asks is, “…do what is good in your eyes.” That leaves it all to David. Ziba comes up, but the request is a lot more open than that.

explanations.answer: Give back all of his land
explanations.explanation: Mephibosheth never asks for his land back. After calling the king like the angel of God, he says, “…so do what is good in your eyes.” He leaves the choice with David. That's a different kind of request than a demand.

Table is right. Mephibosheth says the king set him “among those who eat at your table.” David had told him he would always eat at his table (2 Samuel 9:7). So he's reminding the king of a seat he was already given.
No gate here, friend. Nobody gets set among those who eat at a gate. The verse says Mephibosheth was set among those who eat at the king's table.
A camp sounds like a tent and a long walk. The verse puts him somewhere better. He says the king set him among those who eat at his table.
Divide is right. David says, “I hereby declare that you and Ziba are to divide the land.” Two men and one piece of land, split between them. Mephibosheth is about to answer that.
David says nothing about selling. His words are, “I hereby declare that you and Ziba are to divide the land.” The land stays the land, and it gets split between the two men. No sign out front.
David doesn't tell anyone to leave. He says, “I hereby declare that you and Ziba are to divide the land.” Both men are named in his decision. The word is divide.

That's his answer. Mephibosheth says, “Instead, since my lord the king has safely come to his own house, let Ziba take it all!” The text ties his words to the king getting home safely. I think that says a lot about what mattered to him.

explanations.answer: Give me back all of it
explanations.explanation: It goes the other way. Mephibosheth doesn't ask for all of it back. He says, “Instead, since my lord the king has safely come to his own house, let Ziba take it all!” He hands everything over to Ziba.

explanations.answer: Let the king keep it all
explanations.explanation: The king isn't the one he names. Mephibosheth says, “…let Ziba take it all!” That's a man who answers David's split by offering the whole thing to someone else. He does it right after saying the king has come home safely.

True. The text says that since Barzillai was a very wealthy man, he had provided for the king while he stayed in Mahanaim. So when the king needed help there, Barzillai had it covered. Barzillai the Gileadite was a man the king could count on.

The text says the opposite. Barzillai was a very wealthy man, and “…he had provided for the king while he stayed in Mahanaim.” So Barzillai was the one who provided. That's why David has something to say to him next.

Jerusalem is right. David says, “Cross over with me, and I will provide for you at my side in Jerusalem.” Barzillai had provided for the king, and now the king offers to provide for him. That's the offer on the table.

Close to a lot of Bible stories, but not this one. David says, “Cross over with me, and I will provide for you at my side in Jerusalem.” The place he names is Jerusalem. Barzillai answers by asking about going up to Jerusalem.

Bethlehem is a famous name, but David doesn't use it here. He says, “Cross over with me, and I will provide for you at my side in Jerusalem.” That's the place. And Barzillai's reply is about going up to Jerusalem.

That's the one. Barzillai asks, “Why should your servant be an added burden to my lord the king?” Here's a man who just provided for the king, and he's worried about weighing him down. I think he doesn't want to make himself the center of attention.
Barzillai never pitches himself as an advisor. He asks, “Why should your servant be an added burden to my lord the king?” He doesn't oversell himself at all. It's a short line, and it says it all.

He doesn't offer to be a guide, friend. Barzillai says, “Why should your servant be an added burden to my lord the king?” He asks what he'd be, and the word he picks is burden. He's not trying to impress anybody.
True. Barzillai says, “Your servant will go with the king only a short distance past the Jordan…” So he'll walk a little way with David and no farther. It's a short trip, and he says so himself.
The text says it is true. Barzillai says, “Your servant will go with the king only a short distance past the Jordan…” He won't go on to Jerusalem. He'll go just that short distance.

explanations.answer: To die in his own city near his parents' tomb
explanations.explanation: That's his reason. Barzillai says, “Please let your servant return, that I may die in my own city near the tomb of my father and mother.” He asks for a spot near his parents' tomb. I think it's a quiet, honest thing to ask.

explanations.answer: To look after his flocks out in Gilead
explanations.explanation: Flocks never come up. Barzillai says, “Please let your servant return, that I may die in my own city near the tomb of my father and mother.” His reason is about his own city and his parents' tomb. Nothing about sheep.

explanations.answer: To get his fields ready for the harvest
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't mention fields or a harvest. Barzillai says, “Please let your servant return, that I may die in my own city near the tomb of my father and mother.” That's his reason, in his own words. It's quieter than a to-do list.

explanations.answer: Take him across and do him good
explanations.explanation: That's what he asks. Barzillai says, “Let him cross over with my lord the king, and do for him what is good in your sight.” Chimham is the man he puts forward in his place. Barzillai stays home, but he sends someone along.

explanations.answer: Make him captain of the guard
explanations.explanation: Barzillai doesn't ask for a title. He says, “Let him cross over with my lord the king, and do for him what is good in your sight.” That leaves the details to David. A captain's hat would've been a lot of ask.

explanations.answer: Send him home with gold and silver
explanations.explanation: No gold and silver in this request. Barzillai asks for Chimham to cross over with the king, and for David to do for him what is good in his sight. Chimham goes with David, not home. And Barzillai has just said he doesn't need a reward himself.

David says yes. He answers, “Chimham will cross over with me, and I will do for him what is good in your sight…” He even adds that he will do for Barzillai whatever he desires. So Barzillai's request isn't turned down.
False. David says, “Chimham will cross over with me, and I will do for him what is good in your sight…” Then he adds that he will do for Barzillai whatever he desires. It's a yes, and then some.
That's it. The text says, “The king kissed Barzillai and blessed him, and Barzillai returned home.” A kiss and a blessing, and then he goes home. That's a warm goodbye.
The text doesn't mention a robe. It says the king kissed Barzillai and blessed him, and then Barzillai returned home. Some of the best gifts in the Bible come with no wrapping at all.
The verse doesn't say anything about guards. It says David kissed Barzillai and blessed him, and Barzillai returned home. That's the whole goodbye. I'd say it's simple and it counts.

Half is right. The text says, “All the troops of Judah and half the troops of Israel escorted the king.” So Judah came in full, and Israel only half. Hold on to that, friend, because it matters in the next verses.
Not a third. The text says, “All the troops of Judah and half the troops of Israel escorted the king.” Half is the number. Judah's all of them, and Israel's only half.
Ten does show up in this passage, but later. Israel says, “We have ten shares in the king…” That's a different thing. For the troops escorting the king, the text says half the troops of Israel.

explanations.answer: Judah took the king across secretly
explanations.explanation: That's the complaint. The men of Israel ask, “Why did our brothers, the men of Judah, take you away secretly and bring the king and his household across the Jordan, together with all of David's men?” Nobody likes finding out the party started without them. And you can hear that in their question.

explanations.answer: The king took too long to come back
explanations.explanation: Nothing about the king being slow. Israel's complaint is about Judah. They ask, “Why did our brothers, the men of Judah, take you away secretly…” That's the whole problem for them.

explanations.answer: The king left them out of his army
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say that. The men of Israel are upset about Judah, and they ask why the men of Judah took the king away secretly. They don't say a word about an army. Their question is aimed at their brothers.
That's their reason. The men of Judah answer, “We did this because the king is our relative.” Then they ask why that angers Israel. It's a short answer, and they give it plainly.
They don't say that. The men of Judah say, “We did this because the king is our relative.” Their reason is about family, not about who fought hardest. They don't brag about the fighting.

explanations.answer: They lived closest to the river
explanations.explanation: The river never comes up in their answer. The men of Judah say, “We did this because the king is our relative.” Their reason is the family tie. It's not a map argument.

That's not what they say. They ask, “Have we ever eaten at the king's expense or received anything for ourselves?” It's a question, and I think they're pointing the other direction. They're saying they haven't gotten anything out of this.

False. The men of Judah ask, “Have we ever eaten at the king's expense or received anything for ourselves?” They ask it as a question, and I think the answer they want is no. They're saying they haven't taken a thing.
That's their point. The men of Israel say, “Were we not the first to speak of restoring our king?” They're saying they spoke up first. It's one more reason they think they deserve a say.

explanations.answer: Stand with the king in battle
explanations.explanation: Battle isn't what they bring up. The men of Israel say, “Were we not the first to speak of restoring our king?” Their claim is about speaking first. It's not about who stood where in a fight.
No gifts in this argument. The men of Israel say, “Were we not the first to speak of restoring our king?” That's the point they make. It's about who spoke first.
True. The text says, “But the men of Judah spoke more fiercely than the men of Israel.” Israel came in loud, and Judah turned it up. That volume knob just snapped off.
The text says it is true. It says, “But the men of Judah spoke more fiercely than the men of Israel.” So Israel was hot, and Judah was hotter. It's a heated end to this passage.
